t: Longest Subarray With at Most K Distinct Prime Factors
o: Each number contributes a set of distinct primes; a subarray is valid when the union of these sets has size <= k. We need the longest valid contiguous window. Example 1: [6,10,12] unions to {2,3,5} (size 3) — length 3. Example 3 shows windows can be forced down to single elements. Values go up to 10⁵, so factorization must be fast: precompute smallest prime factors (SPF) with a sieve, giving O(log v) factorization per element. Then it's a textbook sliding window maintaining a prime-count map.
k: Precompute smallest prime factors with a sieve so each number factorizes in O(log v).
Sliding window with a hash map counting occurrences of each prime; validity = map size <= k.
Shrink from the left whenever adding an element pushes distinct primes above k; the window boundaries only move forward, giving linear time.

a.n: Approach 1: Sliding Window with Prime Count Map
a.i: Distinct-prime-count is monotone under expansion/shrinkage, so the classic two-pointer pattern applies: extend the right edge, add the new number's primes, and while distinct primes exceed k, remove primes of the left element and advance the left edge. Track the maximal valid window length.
s: Factorize each element into its distinct primes on the fly.
Two pointers: expand right, add primes to a counter map; while map size > k, remove left element's primes and advance left.
Answer is the max (right - left + 1) observed while valid; 0 if no valid window exists.
a.t: O(M log M + n log V) where M = max value (sieve) and each element factorizes in O(log V) twice (add/remove); window pointers move monotonically.
a.sp: O(M) for the SPF sieve plus O(P) for the prime counter (at most ~6 distinct primes per number, so the map stays tiny).

w: The key framing insight is that 'union of prime sets <= k' behaves exactly like 'at most k distinct characters', enabling the standard sliding window. Pitfalls: naive trial division per query is too slow across 10⁵ elements — always sieve SPF; remember to store counts (not just presence) so removal works; k >= 1 guarantees single-element windows usually exist, but if every element has more than k distinct primes the answer is legitimately 0. Follow-ups: count the number of valid subarrays instead of the longest, or handle updates to the array.
